reasons: GitHub caps every OAuth app at 2,000 access token requests per hour, and going over it blocks new tokens for everyone on that app. Composio's managed GitHub connections run on one shared OAuth app, so other Composio customers' sign-ins count against the same cap as yours. Railway reported a multi-day GitHub login outage in January 2026 after hitting this limit. Your own app gives you your own 2,000.
Your users see your app name on GitHub's consent screen, and in the organization approval request their org owner reviews, instead of Composio's shared app.
GitHub grants rate limit increases per OAuth app, so any increase you negotiate only exists on an app you own.

API call quotas are not the problem here: GitHub counts API calls against each user's own 5,000-per-hour limit, whichever app makes them, so a shared app does not pool API quota the way it pools token requests.

verdict.summary: Self-serve with no review: you can register an OAuth app, test it and open it to any GitHub user in under an hour, the same day. What can block you is on the customer side: organizations have OAuth app access restrictions on by default, so a user's org repos stay out of reach until an owner of that org approves your app, and GitHub gives you no way to speed that up. Also check that refresh works, because new OAuth apps now get access tokens that expire after 8 hours.

timeToProduction.label: Same day for personal repos. Org repos: whenever each customer's org owner approves your app, which you do not control

verdict.mainBlocker: Customer organizations with OAuth app access restrictions (the default for new orgs): until an org owner approves your app, it can only see that org's public resources.

stages.name: Register the OAuth app
limits: GitHub documents no API for creating OAuth apps. This stage has to be done in the browser.
Up to 10 callback URLs per app.
A user or organization can own up to 100 OAuth apps.

steps.title: Decide who owns the app
steps.detail: Register it under your company's GitHub organization, not a personal account, so it does not depend on one person. Apps owned by an organization also get access to that organization's own resources automatically, even with OAuth app access restrictions on.
steps.humanReason: Needs your GitHub sign-in with admin rights on the organization.

steps.title: Create the OAuth app
steps.detail: Go to Settings > Developer settings > OAuth apps > New OAuth App (for an org: the org's Settings > Developer settings). Fill in the application name your users will see, your homepage URL and a short description. Everything here is public, so do not use internal URLs. Composio's own walkthrough shows example values (composio_github_connector, https://composio.dev/): do not copy those, use your own product's. Leave Enable Device Flow off; Composio's browser flow does not need it.
steps.humanReason: Requires your GitHub sign-in, and GitHub offers no API for creating OAuth apps.

preparedValues.label: Application name
preparedValues.value: <Your product name> (shown on the consent screen)

steps.title: Set the callback URL
steps.detail: Paste Composio's redirect URI into Authorization callback URL. Copy it from your Composio GitHub auth config. Do not copy it from Composio's GitHub walkthrough: its screenshots show an older /api/v1/ callback, and the guide itself says to use whatever your current auth config shows. GitHub requires an exact match unless you turn on wildcard matching, which you do not need here and should leave off.

preparedValues.label: Authorization callback URL
preparedValues.value: Copy from Composio: Auth Configs > Create Auth Config > GitHub > OAuth2

steps.title: Decide on expiring tokens
steps.detail: Expire user access tokens is ticked by default on new OAuth apps (since August 2026). Tokens then last 8 hours and come with a refresh token that lasts 6 months. Keep it ticked only if Composio refreshes GitHub tokens for your auth config; Composio does not say whether it does. If you untick it, tokens are long-lived but GitHub revokes any token unused for a year. Test either way (see the next stage).
steps.humanReason: A setting in your signed-in GitHub app registration.

steps.title: Register, then copy the Client ID and generate a Client Secret
steps.detail: Click Register application. On the app page, copy the Client ID and generate a client secret. Copy the secret straight into Composio: it is reported to be shown only once.
steps.humanReason: The secret should only pass from your GitHub settings to Composio.

stages.name: Connect it in Composio and test

duration.label: 5-15 min, plus an 8-hour wait to confirm refresh

limits: Each user can hold at most 10 tokens per app and scope set; GitHub revokes the oldest beyond that.
Signing the same user in 10 times in an hour forces a re-authorization prompt.
Users can grant fewer scopes than you request.

steps.title: Create the GitHub auth config in Composio
steps.detail: Create an OAuth2 auth config for GitHub, turn on Use your own developer credentials and paste the Client ID and Secret. Trim the scopes to what your agent's tools need. OAuth apps have no fine-grained permissions: any tool that touches issues, pull requests or code needs repo, which grants full access to every private repository the user can reach.

preparedValues.label: Scopes in Composio's example
preparedValues.value: repo user gist notifications project workflow codespace

preparedValues.label: Read-only identity and org list (no repo access)

steps.title: Connect your own GitHub account
steps.detail: Start a connection, approve the consent screen and run one read tool (for example, list repositories for the authenticated user). The account needs a verified primary email, or GitHub refuses to issue a token.
steps.humanReason: You approve the consent screen with your own GitHub account.

steps.title: Confirm the connection survives token expiry
steps.detail: If you kept expiring tokens on, run a tool again more than 8 hours after connecting. If it fails with an auth error, Composio did not refresh the token: untick Expire user access tokens in GitHub and reconnect (existing tokens keep their old behaviour until the user signs in again).

stages.name: Open it to your users

duration.label: Same day. Org access waits on each customer's org owner

limits: No review, listing or publish switch: any GitHub user can authorize the app as soon as it exists.
2,000 access token requests per hour for the whole app. Going over it temporarily blocks new tokens for every user.
API calls count against each user's own 5,000 requests per hour, shared with every other app and token that user has (15,000 for members of GitHub Enterprise Cloud orgs that own or approved the app).
Secondary limits: at most 80 content-creating requests per minute and 500 per hour, and 900 points per minute per REST endpoint.

steps.title: Nothing to submit
steps.detail: GitHub has no review or verification step for OAuth apps. A GitHub Marketplace listing is optional and only adds discovery; publisher verification is only needed to sell paid plans.

steps.title: Tell users how to get org access approved
steps.detail: When an org has OAuth app access restrictions, a member authorizes your app for their personal account, then goes to Settings > Applications > Authorized OAuth Apps, opens your app and clicks Request access next to the org. An org owner approves it under the org's Settings > Third-party Access > OAuth app policy. Reconnecting in Composio does not get around this. If the org uses SAML SSO, the user also needs an active SSO session when they authorize.

steps.title: Optional: use a GitHub App instead
steps.detail: GitHub recommends GitHub Apps over OAuth apps: fine-grained permissions, per-repository access and short-lived tokens, and they are not subject to OAuth app access restrictions (an org owner or repo admin installs them instead). Composio accepts your own GitHub App's Client ID and Secret, but it does not hand users the installation link, so you have to send it yourself, and permissions come from the app's settings, not from Composio scopes.
steps.humanReason: Registering a GitHub App needs your GitHub sign-in.

links.label: Differences between GitHub Apps and OAuth apps

requirements.title: No review, fee, privacy policy or business verification
requirements.detail: GitHub asks only for an app name, homepage URL and callback URL. All of it is shown publicly.

requirements.title: Exact callback URL match
requirements.detail: The redirect URI Composio sends must match a registered callback URL exactly, unless wildcard matching is on.

requirements.title: Token handling
requirements.detail: New apps issue 8-hour access tokens with 6-month refresh tokens by default; each refresh returns a new pair and invalidates the old one. Long-lived tokens (if you untick expiry) are revoked after a year without use.

requirements.title: Users need a verified primary email
requirements.detail: Accounts without one cannot authorize any OAuth app.

blockers.title: User connects but cannot see their organization's repos
blockers.symptom: Personal repos work; org repos are missing or return 404, and org listings only show public data.
blockers.fix: The org has OAuth app access restrictions. The user requests access for the org under Settings > Applications > Authorized OAuth Apps, and an org owner approves it. Reconnecting does not help.

blockers.title: Redirect URI not associated with this application
blockers.symptom: GitHub shows 'The redirect_uri is not associated with this application' or returns redirect_uri_mismatch.
blockers.fix: Make the callback URL in GitHub identical to the redirect URI in your Composio auth config. Copy it from the Composio dashboard, not from the screenshots in older guides.

blockers.title: Connection dies after about 8 hours
blockers.symptom: Tool calls start failing with 401 errors the same day the user connected.
blockers.fix: The app issues expiring tokens and the refresh did not happen. Ask Composio whether it refreshes GitHub tokens; if not, untick Expire user access tokens in the app's settings and have users reconnect.

blockers.title: Sign-ins fail for everyone at once
blockers.symptom: New connections and token requests fail during busy periods, then recover.
blockers.fix: The app passed 2,000 access token requests in an hour. Avoid reconnect loops and repeated sign-ins, and move off the shared managed app so other customers' traffic is not counted against you.

blockers.title: 403 or 429 errors on writes
blockers.symptom: Creating issues, comments or pull requests fails with a secondary rate limit message.
blockers.fix: Slow down content-creating calls (80 per minute, 500 per hour) and honour the retry-after header.

blockers.title: unverified_user_email
blockers.symptom: The token request fails with 'The user must have a verified primary email.'
blockers.fix: The user verifies their primary email in GitHub and reconnects.

blockers.title: Application suspended
blockers.symptom: Users are sent back with error=application_suspended.
blockers.fix: GitHub suspended the app for reported abuse, spam or API misuse. Contact GitHub Support.

agentCan: Pick the minimum scopes for the Composio GitHub tools you use
Prepare the app name, homepage URL and description to paste into GitHub
Create the Composio auth config through Composio's API once you give it the Client ID and Secret through a secure channel
Run the 8-hour refresh check and report whether you need to turn token expiry off
Write the help-centre note telling your users how to request org approval, and the note for their org owners
Run tools through Composio rather than reading tokens, since Composio redacts provider tokens from connected-account responses
youMust: Sign in and register the OAuth app under your organization (GitHub documents no API for this)
Generate and hand over the client secret
Approve the first consent screen to test
Accept that each customer's org owner, not you, decides whether your app can reach their org's repos

unknowns.question: Does Composio refresh expiring GitHub OAuth app tokens for custom auth configs?
unknowns.whyItMatters: New GitHub OAuth apps issue 8-hour tokens by default. If Composio does not refresh them, every connection breaks after 8 hours.
unknowns.draftEmail: Hi Composio team, since August 2026 new GitHub OAuth apps issue access tokens that expire after 8 hours, with refresh tokens. If we use our own GitHub OAuth app with expiring tokens enabled, does Composio refresh the token automatically, or should we turn token expiry off? Does the managed GitHub app use expiring tokens? Thanks.

unknowns.question: Do refresh-token requests count toward GitHub's 2,000 access token requests per hour?
unknowns.whyItMatters: With 8-hour tokens, every active user triggers a refresh about three times a day. If refreshes count, the cap fills faster as you grow.
unknowns.draftEmail: Hi GitHub team, our OAuth app uses expiring user access tokens. Do refresh_token grant requests to /login/oauth/access_token count toward the 2,000 access token requests per hour limit for OAuth apps? And how do we request a higher limit for our app? Thanks.

unknowns.question: What scopes does Composio's GITHUB toolkit request by default?
unknowns.whyItMatters: Composio's walkthrough only lists the scopes from its example screenshot. repo alone grants full private repository access, which some org owners will refuse to approve.
unknowns.askWhom: Your Composio dashboard (the GitHub auth config's default scopes), or Composio support
unknowns.draftEmail: Hi Composio team, which OAuth scopes does the GitHub toolkit request by default, and which tools stop working if we drop repo and use only public_repo or read:org? Thanks.

unknowns.question: How does GitHub decide on rate limit increases for an OAuth app?
unknowns.whyItMatters: GitHub says increases are granted per OAuth app, but publishes no process or criteria.
unknowns.draftEmail: Hi GitHub team, GitHub's docs say rate limit increases are granted per OAuth app. What is the process to request one, and what do you need from us? Thanks.

sources.title: GitHub Docs: Authorizing OAuth apps
sources.quote: The access token expires after eight hours, and the refresh token expires after six months without use.

sources.title: GitHub Docs: Differences between GitHub Apps and OAuth apps
sources.quote: OAuth app tokens re long-lived by default.

claims.text: GitHub revokes an OAuth token that has not been used in one year, and any valid token pushed to a public repository or gist.

sources.title: GitHub Docs: Token expiration and revocation
sources.quote: GitHub will automatically revoke an OAuth token or personal access token when the token hasn't been used in one year.

claims.text: GitHub issues at most ten tokens per user/application/scope combination and ten tokens per hour; going over the count revokes an older token, and signing a user in ten times in an hour forces re-authorization.

sources.title: GitHub Docs: Token expiration and revocation
sources.quote: There is a limit of ten tokens that are issued per user/application/scope combination, and a rate limit of ten tokens created per hour.

sources.title: GitHub Docs: Rate limits for OAuth apps
sources.quote: If an app signs the user in ten times within one hour, the next sign in within the same hour will require re-authorization of the application.

claims.text: OAuth apps are limited to 2,000 access token requests per hour; beyond that new token requests are temporarily blocked, which GitHub warns can cause outages.

sources.title: GitHub Docs: Rate limits for OAuth apps
sources.quote: OAuth apps are subject to a rate limit of 2,000 access token requests per hour.

claims.text: API requests made with an OAuth app token count against the user's own 5,000 requests per hour, combined with every other app and token acting for that user; members of a GitHub Enterprise Cloud org that owns or approved the app get 15,000.

sources.quote: This rate limit is combined with any requests that another GitHub App or OAuth app makes on that user's behalf and any requests that the user makes with a personal access token.

sources.title: GitHub Docs: Differences between GitHub Apps and OAuth apps
sources.quote: OAuth tokens use the user's rate limit of 5,000 requests per hour.

sources.title: GitHub Docs: Differences between GitHub Apps and OAuth apps
